Schizophrenia: Long-Term Care

psychosocial care and relapse preventionWhat is driving this relapse or limiting recovery, and which added treatment answers it?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Danger to himself or others hospitalize, involuntarily if necessary
  • Antipsychotic continues in every patient psychosocial treatment added to it
  • Worse while taking his doses ask what changed: family conflict family therapy first, a higher dose after
What it is

Maintenance care after the first episode: fewer relapses and admissions, better quality of life

Driver

Stress in a vulnerable patient can bring symptoms back support, coping skills and the antipsychotic may buffer it

Triggers

Stopping the antipsychotic (most relapse within 12 months of a first episode)

Critical, hostile or overinvolved family substance use, especially cannabis

Job or income loss, leaving home for college, a breakup, joining the Armed Forces

Chain

Missed doses, conflict or drugs relapse admission may be needed if severe

Function may decline over the first 5 years then plateaus

Insights

Worse while taking every dose what changed in his life, not the drug, comes first

Family conflict more stress voices take on darker meaning, less reserve to cope

Long-term course, stage by stagedetail behind the chain
First yearOutcome tracks adherence to medication and avoiding illicit drugs
MaintenanceContinuous use, with long-acting forms, can bring 1-year relapse to about 30% or loweraims: fewer recurrences and admissions, better quality of life
RecoverySkill training and vocational programs help many work, shop, care for themselves and get along with others
MortalityPoor diet, weight gain, smoking and substance use shorten life by about 13 to 15 years
OutcomeAbout 15% to 25% recover; about a third improve but relapse or keep some disability; up to 40% do poorly
PrognosisBetter: good premorbid function, late or sudden onset, few negative symptoms, short untreated psychosisworse: young onset, poor premorbid function, family history of schizophrenia, many negative symptoms
2Urgent risks
DangerDanger to himself or others, eg a voice commanding harm plus a hidden weapon
APA positionA mental disorder makes harm to self or others, or unmet basic needs, likely; hospital care can help; he is unable or unwilling to consent; it is the least restrictive option. Commitment law varies by state.

If he is a danger and refuses admission, choose hospitalization, involuntary if necessary; safety before family therapy.

SuicideLifetime suicide risk 5% to 10% in schizophrenia

If he is a danger to himself, choose hospitalization, involuntary if necessary.

3Differential
Why is he relapsing, most tempting first
DriverFingerprintDecides it
Family conflict or high expressed emotionCriticism, hostility or overinvolvement; he takes his dosesConflict just before the worsening; family therapy first, as an outpatient, then a dose change
NonadherenceMissed or forgotten oral doses or refillsPoor or uncertain adherence, not a failed drug; long-acting injectable
Poor engagement with servicesMissed injections or visits with frequent admissions, homelessness or legal troubleHistory of poor engagement behind the relapses; assertive community treatment
Mood symptoms with the psychosisMood episodes for most of the illness (criteria in Psychosis)
Voices persist on adequate doses2 or more adequate trials fail, adherence documented
Especially cannabis or hallucinogensUse before the recurrence; strongly discourage it: it predicts a poor outcome
Other life stressorLost job or income, left home, a breakupA non-family stressor just before the worsening; treat it first, the drug continues
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Anxious and jitteryDistress, not the causeLorazepam may ease anxiety; it treats neither the psychosis nor its cause
Never a manic or depressive episodeSchizophrenia, not schizoaffectiveNo lithium: unhelpful in schizophrenia
Not dangerous; a stressor drives the relapseOutpatient careNo partial hospital program or clozapine at this point

Pause point. The bait: a higher dose, clozapine or lithium for voices that rose after a family argument in a patient receiving his injections. The conflict came just before the worsening, so family therapy comes first and a dose change follows.

7Treatment
1

Alwaysevery patient, once improved

Continue the antipsychotic
2

Nextworse on his doses, with a stressor just before

Treat the stressor as an outpatient: family therapy for a family conflict

Not dangerous: a partial hospital program is not needed now.

3

Thenstressor treated, voices still more frequent

A higher dose or dosing frequency

A switch to clozapine is not needed yet.

Match the added treatment to the problem
SituationChooseWatch for
Ongoing contact with family, or a critical familyFamily intervention: psychoeducation, understanding, communication, coping skillsCochrane reviewIt may cut relapses and admissions and help him take his medication; the trials were weak, so the benefit may be overstated.
Poor or uncertain adherence, or he prefers itLong-acting injectable antipsychoticNot for a patient already receiving his injections
Missed injections or visits with frequent relapse, homelessness or legal troubleWhat it isA team with many staff per patient brings all or nearly all care to his home or residence.
Wants competitive paid work, even if now in a sheltered workshopSupported employment: a competitive job with an on-site coach
Residual voices or delusions despite adherence, fewer than 2 failed adequate trialsAdd What it isCognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis, alone or in a group, aimed at lessening delusional thoughts, hallucinations and negative symptoms.
2 or more failed adequate trials, adherence documentedClozapine
Goal of getting along better with othersSocial skills training
Every patientPsychoeducation, with CBT for psychosis and supported employment

APA 2020American Psychiatric Association 2020: recommended for continuing the antipsychotic, psychoeducation, CBT for psychosis, supported employment, assertive community treatment; suggested, the weaker grade, for family intervention, a long-acting injectable, social skills training.

8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Improved on an antipsychoticContinue it; off it, 65% to 80% relapse within 12 months of a first episode
Every visitLook for adherence barriers and early signs of relapse
On any antipsychoticMonitor regularly for metabolic adverse effects
Increased risk of suicide or aggressionClozapine (APA); also approved to prevent suicide in schizophrenia
Practice
  1. 30-year-old man, schizophrenia, monthly aripiprazole injection argued with his parents 1 week ago a voice tells him to stab his father has hidden a kitchen knife in his room Refuses admission T 37.0 °C · HR 92/min · guarded, oriented → Involuntary psychiatric hospitalization → a command to harm his father and a hidden knife are danger to others; he refuses, so admission is involuntary; safety comes before family therapy
  2. 27-year-old man, schizophrenia, haloperidol injection every 3 weeks voices rose after arguments with his parents after 8 weekly family sessions: arguments stopped; parents see an illness voices still more frequent than before Threatens no one vital signs normal · cooperative, oriented → Increase the haloperidol dose or frequency → the stressor has been treated; the next step is a higher dose or dosing frequency, and a switch to clozapine is not necessary at this point
  3. 22-year-old man, schizophrenia, risperidone since a first admission 3 months ago lives with his parents family meeting: mother calls him lazy, says he ruins every holiday father interrupts to list his failures vital signs normal · flat affect · no hallucinations now → Frequent criticism and hostility from his parents → high expressed emotion in the family: criticism, hostility or overinvolvement means more frequent relapses; family intervention answers it
  4. 20-year-old man, schizophrenia, risperidone since a first admission 4 months ago no psychotic symptoms for 6 weeks lives with parents who get along well with him they ask how to prevent another episode vital signs normal · euthymic, oriented, no hallucinations → Psychoeducation sessions for him and his parents → he lives with his family; psychoeducational family interventions can reduce the rate of relapse, and psychoeducation is recommended for every patient
  5. 31-year-old man brought by his sister; schizophrenia oral risperidone 4 years; filled 2 of last 5 monthly prescriptions forgets the pills 2 weeks of voices; believes neighbors spy Lives alone; threatened no one afebrile; toxicology negative · guarded, oriented → Restart risperidone as a long-acting injection → poor adherence, not a failed drug: a long-acting injectable is suggested for poor or uncertain adherence
  6. 38-year-old man, schizophrenia, monthly paliperidone injections missed 3 of last 5 injections 6 months: 2 admissions, 4 emergency visits in a shelter since losing his apartment cannot reach the clinic across town afebrile · calm, oriented · a quiet voice at night → Assertive community treatment → poor engagement with services has led to frequent relapse and homelessness; a team brings nearly all care to where he lives
  7. 29-year-old woman, schizophrenia, aripiprazole for 3 years no psychotic symptoms for 1 year sheltered workshop for 2 years wants a regular paid job at a grocery store Lives with her husband vital signs normal · euthymic, linear thought, no hallucinations → Supported employment with an on-site job coach → she wants competitive work; supported employment places her in a competitive job with a coach and is recommended for every patient
  8. 26-year-old man, schizophrenia, risperidone for 2 years no psychotic symptoms for 8 months part-time job with a coach; takes every dose no friends; avoids conversation at work Goal: getting along with people vital signs normal · blunted affect, linear thought → Social skills training → his stated goal is better social functioning, for which social skills training is suggested; he is already engaged, adherent and working
  9. 34-year-old man, schizophrenia, olanzapine for 2 years every dose taken by pill count still hears a critical voice most days; distressed Lives with a supportive brother; no conflict; no thoughts of harm vital signs normal · toxicology negative · oriented; partial insight → Add cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis → adherent, safe and without a family conflict; this therapy works on hallucinations and delusional thoughts and is recommended for every patient
  10. 36-year-old woman, schizophrenia, risperidone for 5 years still hears voices several times a week never a manic or depressive episode Lives with her parents vital signs normal · euthymic, full affect, oriented → Adding lithium carbonate → no mood episodes: lithium is sometimes used for mood symptoms in schizoaffective disorder but is unhelpful in schizophrenia
  11. 32-year-old woman, schizophrenia, olanzapine since her first episode no psychotic symptoms for 18 months feels well; takes every dose asks to stop the medication Lives with her husband vital signs normal · euthymic, linear thought → Continue olanzapine → symptoms improved on an antipsychotic, so it is continued; without ongoing antipsychotic after a first episode, 65 to 80% relapse within 12 months
How NBME framed it: question 1

27-year-old man with schizophrenia; haloperidol injection every 3 weeks cooperative and friendly, but anxious and jittery 1 week of more frequent voices; job performance suffering Works at a sheltered workshop; lives with his parents argued with them about his illness 10 days ago they repeatedly say that without a regular job he will “never amount to anything” they call the voices an excuse not to meet new people and worry he will never marry

Most appropriate intervention?

Competing answers
  • Partial hospital program: his voices are worse; but it is not necessary now: address the conflict as an outpatient first.
  • Move to a halfway house: it would separate him from critical parents; but it is not appropriate; the explanation notes he has no criminal history.
  • Add lithium carbonate: an add-on drug for a relapse; but it is sometimes used for mood symptoms in schizoaffective disorder and is unhelpful in schizophrenia.
  • Add lorazepam: he looks anxious and jittery; it may ease anxiety but addresses neither the psychosis nor its likely root, the family conflict.
  • Switch haloperidol to clozapine: the voices are breaking through; but a switch is not necessary at this point; the immediate stressor comes first.
  • Increase the haloperidol dose: it targets the voices; but it is a later step, to consider once the family conflict has been addressed.

Down to two: family therapy or adding lithium. Family therapy: family conflict is a risk factor for worsening psychosis, and the argument came just before the voices increased in a patient receiving his injections. Treat that stressor first, as an outpatient; then consider a higher haloperidol dose or frequency.

Pairs with Psychosis covers which psychotic disorder by duration and the antipsychotic ladder up to clozapine; this brief covers what to add around the drug. Here a higher dose or frequency is considered after a treated stressor in a patient already receiving his doses (NBME); the sibling ladder's switch is for no response after an adequate trial. Ask: is the question which disorder, which drug, or what to add?
Transferable rule

Danger to himself or others comes before every other step. When a patient who is receiving his antipsychotic gets worse, ask what changed in his life before changing the drug, and treat that first.
